utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Kyle Wood, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We would like to greet everybody present in the courtroom, Mr. Withopf, Mr. Mundis, and the Defence counsel, as well as the accused, everybody present in the courtroom, court reporters, the interpreters, and security officers. I understand that Mr. Withopf wanted to tell us something at the beginning of today's hearing, but do you want to do it in the presence of the witness or in the absence of the witness? Mr. Mundis, please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. President, the issue that I wanted to briefly raise perhaps might best be done in the presence of the witness. It concerns some documents that he refers to in his report and which we have translated for the benefit of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are, then, going to bring the witness into the courtroom. Usher, can you please go and bring Mr. Reinhardt into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. First I would like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything is all right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. There is a problem in the translation of documents. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's not so much a problem. Let me explain very briefly. General Reinhardt in his report cited to a number of German regulations. When he was last here and at the behest of the Defence, we endeavoured to get those documents translated for the benefit of the Defence. General Reinhardt consequently gave us his copies of those documents. We have since had them translated, and General Reinhardt, when we met with him prior to his testimony, asked that those documents be returned to him following the translation so that he would have them available in the event he was questioned with respect to those German regulations and since he had given us his only copy. And I would simply like to ask the usher to show the translations back to the Defence and then for those documents to be returned to General Reinhardt, and I wanted to do that in open court so that I didn't return any documents to the witness in the absence of the Trial Chamber and the Defence. I would also just indicate for the Defence that -- and for General Reinhardt's benefit that the documents, the German regulations that he provided to us, certain portions of them were highlighted by Mr. Withopf for the benefit of the translation service so they would know which passages needed to be translated. So I would ask if the usher could perhaps show those documents to the Defence and then return them to General Reinhardt. That's what I would like to just call to your attention. And again, the markings on the documents were made by the Prosecution in order to direct the interpretation services to which portions of the documents needed to be translated. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So may the document be given to the Defence for their possible comments. Any comments on behalf of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. We don't have any comments, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No comments for us either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are going to continue with the cross-examination. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Reinhardt.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I had a few questions for you which were remaining from yesterday's part of my cross-examination, but I prefer to -- because we're limited on time, to move straight on into the first substantive part, and that was going over some of your qualifications in order to help the Trial Chamber, as I've mentioned yesterday. So the first question I have for you this morning - and I refer to your -- to your -- the information you have provided the Trial Chamber in your document concerning your career, and you said that you had -- you began your military career in 1960 but that you had done the first five years of your military career as a platoon leader. Can you confirm for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that as a platoon leader this is where you learned the basic tenets of leadership and the difficulties of leading young soldiers into the military profession.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you elaborate, in terms of what as a junior officer and a platoon leader is the focus of the platoon leader in leading his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a double focus. One focus is that you train your soldiers to become perfect in their profession, and I commanded, for instance, the High Mountain Platoon of my battalion, where we have all the mountain specialists. You train them in their mountain training, in their skiing and military training. And the second aspect is that you take care of the well-being of your soldiers. And I think this is as important as -- as the professional thing, as training, because if they don't feel being treated accordingly, you cannot train them accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, could you confirm that even though a platoon leader can be identified as being a junior leader in the scale of the officer profession, that nevertheless a platoon leader is of the utmost importance for the soldiers of the platoon and that they would look to the platoon leader as in accordance to the principle of unity of command basically the people, they will always look up to for anything they need, in terms of their profession?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. The platoon leader is the incorporation of the army for the refugee -- for the recruit, for the individual soldier. He represents the whole organisation for him, because he is the guy he is constantly in touch with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I move on to the next part in your career, where in 1967 you were sent to the university to go into studies of history and political science and where you ended up doing your thesis. Now, I -- hoping to find some material, I did get a copy of your thesis, and I did not find what I was looking for in terms of command and control but I did find some very interesting material in terms of your thesis and entitled, "Moscow: The Turning Point? The Failure of Hitler's Strategy in the Winter of 1941-1942." I have not read all of it, General, to be honest, but I have one quick question concerning one of the things you referred to constantly in your thesis is the problems due to the economy and the problems due to the armament industry. Could you confirm that armament industry and the lack of weapons or the difficulty in order to obtain the proper weapons to wage war and economic difficulties are indeed very important issues for a commander.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that the armament industry is very important for the commander, but the output of the armament industry. If he doesn't have the appropriate armament, if he hasn't -- if he doesn't have the appropriate weapons systems, it's difficult for him to fight an enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on, General, to -- in terms of 1974-1975, when you attend the command and general staff officer course. Can you confirm that this is the course where one is usually selected to attend because potential has been identified in the junior officer to attend more senior ranks and that this is to go for the ranks usually of a lieutenant colonel to colonel?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is a -- a course which you run through before in a selection course, and only 10 per cent of a year group are then selected, based on different tests you run through for a whole year. And then you attend the General Staff College, which is the key -- the key institution which qualifies you for colonel and above.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in 1975, you had the opportunity, General, to attend a similar type of course, which is the United States Command and Staff College at Fort Leavenworth. Now, would you agree with me that attending this course did turn out to be a major issue in your career because of all the Americans that you met there, all the officers from other countries, and a chance to discuss the doctrine of the United States and to compare it with your own?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was the key thing. I don't believe that I learned very much more, but the comparison about the way of achieving your goals, that there is not only one way but different ways to be successful or not successful and to get in touch with soldiers from all over the world - we were some thousand students, about 120 foreign students - was the key for me to attend this course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in 1976, General, you moved on to headquarters CENTAG in Heidelberg, and where you -- what I have down but I think that you said something, you might have said something differently yesterday. What I have down from your document was that you were the G3 staff officer. Can you please confirm that this, the G3, is the person who deals with operations and what were your duties in CENTAG?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duties were to write the general defence plan for the southern part of Germany, i.e., from the area of Kassel south to the mountains for all the forces operating into this -- in this area; i.e., the German, the Belgian, the American, and the French forces, to come up with the consolidated defence plan for the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's when during this period I take it somewhere between 1976 and 1980 you became military assistant to the vice-Chief of Staff of the German Army. Would I be correct in saying that from that point on you really were dealing with issues at the operational level and even at the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's been somewhere in between, because the vice-chief of the German armed forces is responsible for the planning of the military structure, the military operation of the Bundeswehr in comparison to the budget available, and I was his key assistant in this planning process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Ask then in 1983, or I guess for a period of, I think, something like three years, you were personally selected by Dr. Manfred Worner to become his senior military assistant when he was Minister of Defence. During that time frame, could you confirm that you indeed dealt with strategic issues?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, of course you commanded following this assignment with the Minister of Defence, you commanded a brigade of 6.000 men.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that this is the ultimate command position for a military commander, a land force military commander, in terms of where he still has direct input with the men, and -- if I compare with the higher assignment, and at the same time he is a very senior officer?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have put it in a better way, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In 1988, you moved and your career took a bit of a -- of a move towards when you became a Brigadier General, and you were then the deputy Chief of Staff plans for the German Armed Forces. Some of the things you dealt with, according to the information we have been provided with, includes procurement, structure, and the reorganisation of the German Armed Forces. My first question deals with procurement. Can you give a brief description of the difficulties encountered in the procurement of military equipment in your own experience.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There are a couple of major problems, but the key problem is that the -- the requirements of the military are normally exceeding the budget possibilities of the country, so the question is how to cope with the requirements on the one side and the budget, on the other side, to come up with the consolidated plan, which satisfies the requirements of the forces. The second big thing is that amongst the forces, the requirements of the different services, like army, navy, air force, medical service, and so on, are contradicting itself, because they all ask for a bigger share, which normally can be paid only at the expense of their brother services. And to harmonise this internally within the military and then with the government, with the -- with the finance minister and the chancellor is a hell of a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can you elaborate a bit more in terms of -- and we'll come back to this later, but the idea of procurement as you've just described it, of course you were talking in peacetime. Could you comment on what it could be like in a combat situation if your own state was at war.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very difficult, Mr. Bourgon, because the whole procurement process was geared at that time not toward peacetime but toward deployment operations, because at that time we still had our problem with the Warsaw Pact. We were ready to deploy within 48 hours to defend Germany and the Alliance, so we were not talking peacetime. We were talking preparation for the worse case. And therefore, everything was geared on -- on fighting forces and make them ready the best way to train, to fight them, and give them the best materiel. You know, today the modern equipment is so complicated, it's so complex that what you don't have available at the beginning will never reach you at the end any more, at least in this very modern and high operation speed warfare, so you had to procure in anticipation what could happen very much in detail what you needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the second part of my question relates to the reorganisation of the German Armed Forces. Now, this was the period 1988 and 1990. Could you confirm that as part of the German Army, but also if you have the knowledge, compared to other armies, that this was a significant period for the military in many parts of the world in terms of reorganisation due to economical factors and the world economy, that at that point on many armed forces in the world were reorganising?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were undergoing a very special situation by that time. We had to reorganise our forces the way you just explained it; i.e., reducing the forces, making them more modern, reducing them from 480.000 to about 370, 380.000. At the same time, having been forced to do that, you remember that we had the unification of Germany, and the question came up how to -- how to deal with the East German national army, which was more than 100.000 personnel which had to be somehow amalgamated with the West German Army, and I think this was a unique situation no country ever had done before, and we had no precedence to do that and we had to plan on this in very, very short notice. And -- and to harmonise these two main -- main streams; i.e., reducing the Bundeswehr, on the one hand, and somehow to amalgamate the two parts, two very antagonistic parts of the armed forces was a very difficult endeavour. And I must say that I never encountered in my career such a difficult time than this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you confirm, General, that this experience gave you both the knowledge and a feel for the -- the utmost difficulties in military reorganisation, whether it is in downsizing or increasing the military?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I already said yesterday, this is a very, very difficult part. And if you have to do this in an unorganised fashion -- we were in a rather happy situation, because there was no war going on. So even under the political pressure and the military pressure, we could -- we could do our business in a rather normal way. Even so we worked day and nights. But we were not attacked by anybody, so it was easier for us. But nevertheless, it was a very, very difficult task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, could you -- you've touched upon this issue yesterday, and again we'll come back to it, but could you relate this situation to that of a newborn state trying to build its own military.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was by that time pretty often in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was very, very sorry for my brothers in arms, having to deal on the one hand with fighting an enemy and, on the other hand, to become independent and to build up their own organic armed forces. I must say that this was very difficult, having seen the country in a very destroyed way, having seen all these refugees. I remember rebuilding the bridge in Visoko with my forces over the Bosna River, being in Kakanj very often. Having all these in mind, it was a total different task and a much more difficult task. The commanders of the ABiH were at that time than we were, even so our tasks we thought were very difficult. For them I think it was very, very difficult to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1990, you were promoted Major General, and you were appointed or assigned as commander of the General Staff and Command College. I take it that this is the same college that you had attended yourself, or was it a different college?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is the highest ranking institution as far as training and education is concerned in the German Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, could you confirm -- you mentioned this in your written statement -- but that you -- the importance of such an institution to build a national military that is effective and that is what you, I guess, referred to as the institutional background.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the melting pot in which you basically have every staff officer or every captain before he becomes a staff officer in the same training to get the proper direction of the armed forces and to prepare them for acting as future senior officers. This is the key institution and the mental backbone of an armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move quickly, General, to 1993, when you are promoted Lieutenant General. And you are assigned as commander of three corps in Koblenz. And you mentioned that your corps was composed of two Panzer Grenadier Division, also 5 and 10 Panzer Division, and 30.000 corps troops, for a total of 90.000 troops. We will get on later with the composition of a corps. Can you confirm that this is one of the largest corps that you commanded and how much of a challenge it was to command this corps and especially to accomplish your mission, which was to take it apart and to disband it and to reorganise it into something else.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the corps was one of the biggest corps in Germany defending the very famous Fulda Gap together with our American friends. It was a very powerful tool, but at the same time, since we were already in the process of reducing the German Armed Forces it had to be disbanded, and out of my three divisions, only elements of one division remained. And I tell you it's much easier to build something up than to disassemble a unit, because it creates a lot of tears, a lot of frustration amongst those who have to give up their battalions, their brigades, their homes and move on, or just lose the job. At the same time, we had to build up a new organisation, because we started with the deployment of German forces to Somalia, and it became obvious that other peacekeeping operations were due in the Balkans, and we need an organisation to organise, to train the people before the deploy and also to command and control them as a national element wherever they went abroad. And therefore I had to transfer my corps staff into a much smaller army forces staff for those out-of-area operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And all the meanwhile, General, can you confirm of course you are dealing with a professional officer corps to help you in doing so.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I -- as I tried to mention yesterday, all the officers which are -- who are being assigned to a corps staff are first class officers. You get the best of -- of your army, because this is the -- one of the key staffs for operations. So they all have been through command training before, they all have commanded companies, all battalions on the senior staff level. They are all handpicked, and I had a big saying in who would serve on my staff or who would not be qualified enough to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to 1994-1998, when you built the German Armed Forces command in Koblenz and that you were kind of the coordinating agency for the Bundeswehr operations abroad. Now, my understanding of this position is that you were kind of the force generator, which means that based on the missions which are taken up by Germany, you would identify the troops who would deploy and ensure that the replacement would be prepared in time to deploy for future deployments.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's more about that, sir. This is not only providing the troops to deploy but much more important is to prepare the troops to -- before they deploy for their particular mission, which is totally different in Somalia from the deployment to Croatia, in UNPROFOR, for instance. You have to prepare them in all the escalatory and de-escalatory means in peacekeeping rather than in fighting, because you don't go there in fighting an enemy; you go there with a purpose of re-creation of normality, of helping people to come back to normality, which is a total different approach. So we trained our ourselves. We basically came up with training systems. And every soldier before he deployed had to undergo a very robust additional training of about six to eight weeks, depending on what he was doing. And I was also responsible for their equipment. And let me tell you that this was not a very easy thing, because I needed special equipment for the security -- for the force protection of my forces. And as I said before, our army always -- the army always is confronted with scarce resources, so the security problem was the key problem, that we don't have too many casualties once we deploy. And this fight for the appropriate equipment, also command and control equipment, was -- was key for the sake of the soldiers who had to deploy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that as the -- in this position you were considered as the national commanders for any German deployment abroad?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you actually deploy with the troops, or were you back in Germany and then visited the troops on and on?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second is the proper thing. I had a commander -- a brigadier commander on the spot, and I was there almost every second week to check and to help and to see how the -- how the operations would go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. So but the -- can you confirm that the overall authority for each of those deployments were -- you were entrusted with this overall responsibility.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was entrusted vis-a-vis the Minister of Defence for the deployment and the well-being of soldiers under my command. And every soldier who deployed abroad came automatically under my command, notwithstanding to which unit he belonged before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I moved -- and I tried to move a bit quicker, because I've got lots of questions, but I think this is important for the Judges to get a good understanding of the military. You mentioned that your employment culminated in 1998-1999, when you became commander of Allied Land Forces Central Europe, or LANDCENT, and in that capacity you played a role in NATO's structural reform and where NATO's tasks were redefined. Can you elaborate on this briefly.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will elaborate very briefly. The key thing by that time was that NATO was too bulky in its staff capabilities. It was too much separated in army, navy, and air force components, and our endeavour was to make it more joined; i.e., to get army, navy, air force more in a synergistic way, introduce staffs in order to streamline, to have less chiefs on the -- on the spot and more indians on the ground, and we tried very hard to reduce the size of our staffs and to compose the staffs and to join staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 1999 you had your -- probably your ultimate assignment - and if I'm wrong, please correct me - when you are assigned as commander of the KFOR or the international peace force in Kosovo. And in that capacity you had to command 50.000 troops from 39 nations, including four Russian battalions and 1200 soldiers even from the United Arabic Republic. Can you elaborate on the challenge of commanding such a force in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the biggest challenge at the beginning was that I had no command and control assets whatsoever. As I elaborated on yesterday, my predecessor, General Jackson, the British general, redeployed his army corps plus all his signal command and control forces, and I had all my command and control assets still in Sarajevo because my staff also acted as the staff of SFOR. And when the staff redeployed, we left all our equipment there. So we had to build a total new command and control system which did not apply only for my own forces but which was used by the United Nations, by the police, and everything, because there was no functioning system in -- in Kosovo by that time. We had to build this up, and then you had those different nations. And I thought it would be a very difficult way to command and control nations of total different doctrines, different religions, different colours in the face, from Argentina to Azerbaijan, but it was easier because all these young soldiers deployed to help people getting back into normality were very eager to do the utmost and trying to help in order to, well, make the situation for the families of -- in the country for the -- for the Albanians and the Serbs better than they used to be during this war before. So the adhesion of those KFOR forces, notwithstanding the nations they belonged to, were much closer and much easier to deal with than I ever anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can confirm, General, that you are -- first -- you have firsthand experience of the difficulties in setting up such a command and control system in a new environment concerning this peace -- international peace mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And based on this experience, you could relate to trying to establish the same thing, where the soldiers you deploy with are either untrained or simply not soldiers at all and the lack of a professional officer corps and in a fighting mode where you are in combat. Could you relate your experience, how difficult it was to this second scenario?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already pointed out in my paper, it must have been very difficult for the commanders, for the leadership in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to build up, to equip, to train the soldiers, and at the same time to fight a double enemy, and it was a hell of a job what they have to do, and it's amazing for me, on the other hand, how operationally successful they were in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And could you confirm, General, that the focus which was on your mind when you were in Kosovo with this challenge that you were facing was definitely your mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But coming back to your last question, the mission was totally different from the one my comrade-in-arms in Bosnia-Herzegovina had because I was not there to fight. I was there to stabilise internally and externally the situation as a prerequisite to build upon this stabilisation a new administration and to improve the economy. If I had had to fight an enemy with the forces at my disposition I would have been in deep trouble, in deep trouble, and I don't know how I would have succeeded in fighting a war-fighting operation with this kind of multinational forces, because they were not fighting forces; they were peacekeeping forces, and it's quite a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to the last part of your career, which is of less application to this case, and where you went back to LANDCENT but then you had to reorganising [sic] into a joint headquarters. I would simply like to -- if you could confirm for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that the joint headquarters is -- when we say "joint," it doesn't deal with multinational but it deals with the three services, and that now all the focus of multinational operations is placed on joint operation, where the navy, the air force, and the army worked together, in terms of an organised system?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's both, sir. First of all, the staff I had is a multinational staff; still is. So I had all NATO nations on the staff, including now the new NATO nations, like the Poles, the Czechs, the Hungarians, which we incorporated in my staff once I redeployed. But the key focus was to basically take harvest of our efforts, which we discussed before, to make a lame staff into a more component staff. So I included some 60 naval -- some 60 air force and some 20 naval and marine officers in my staff, and I had to reduce my army component considerably to have all the knowledge of the services available in my staff to be more effective to fight the way we -- we see today modern warfare developing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity, General, I was wondering if you took part in a big military exercise which took place. It was a command post exercise which took place near Prague in 2000, where it was a big NATO exercise and command post exercise.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not take place in this one, because by that time when this was prepared I was still commander in KFOR. I monitored this, but at that time we still had much more problems in integrating the -- the Czech Army elements into the NATO army, and we trained them differently in my headquarters, but I did not attend that particular exercise in Prague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. This concludes the first part of my cross-examination concerning your background, in terms of dealing with your own experience and helping the Trial Chamber. I move on to the second part. In this part, General, I'd like to basically go over the structure of a corps and to go to the basic elements in order to help the Trial Chamber. I propose to begin with some very basic concepts and to move on to more complicated concepts, but on most occasions I would simply like you to confirm whether you agree with some of the things I will propose to you, and this stuff comes from a doctrine manual, so I guess we could move rather quickly to these -- to these propositions I have for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher, please, to give the following document to the witness and to circulate it around. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, you have a structure, the rank structure within the army. I mean, the land element. Now, even though there are some differences amongst the rank structure from country to country, could you confirm that basically this is the normal rank structure on the left side from the officer side, moving from officer cadet to second lieutenant to lieutenant, captain, major, or in some countries it's called a commandant, lieutenant colonel, colonel, brigadier general, major general, lieutenant general, and four -- full four-star general, which is the rank that you achieved?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the non-commissioned officer side, on the right side of this drawing, where you move from a recruit, a soldier undergoing basic military training, and you move up the scale until you are -- in some countries it's called a warrant officer, like in Canada; in some countries it might be called a senior non-commissioned officer; and then you have different levels of seniority. Would that be the normal structure?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, and I would like it to be marked for identification, please. Can I have a number, Mr. President, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure if Mr. Bourgon wants to tender this into evidence or simply have it marked for identification. The Prosecution has no objection to this document, either being marked for identification or actually being admitted into evidence. It's -- it's up to the Defence and Your Honours, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in that case, can we have an exhibit number straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Registrar, can we have an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number DH135.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] I'd ask the usher to please pass on a second document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This document, General Reinhardt, would I be right in saying that this is, again, taking into account that in some countries it might be somewhat different, that overall this is the basic diagram representing formation in units, in subunits in the land element, moving from a detachment from three to six soldiers, to a section, to a platoon, to a company, to a battalion, a regiment - and where we have "battalion" and "regiment," of course the name differs because sometimes it would be called a regiment in the artillery world - moving to a brigade, a division, and a corps. Would that be the basic order of units and the average size of these units?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you should like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is a basic question for you, General, but the idea behind this -- this sketch, because we are talking in this case of all these units, and to the Defence it is important that we have a good grasp of what is each unit and what it is composed of. Now, I understand that from what you mentioned in your written statement that the size of the units that you could encounter, based on the documents that you've read, might not be exactly these same numbers.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But if I may elaborate, also the size of the numbers of divisions and corps in NATO vary very much amongst each other. I commanded six multinational corps. And every corps looked totally different from the other one because of the multinationality. The size, the composition was totally different. So we have to see this is a term, but what is behind the term, sometimes it's very difficult. Very different also from country to country. And also the same applies to the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to pass on another document. [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President. Could I have a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the -- the document that we now have before us with the -- from corps down to detachment, again, the Prosecution has no objection to this document being tendered with the caveat that I think the Defence put forward as well, that this is more or less a generic structure or that the sizes are generic and are not necessarily specific to the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. But other than that, Mr. President, we have no objection to the document titled, "Formations, units, and Subunits" being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. Madam Registrar, can we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... DH136.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, to illustrate exactly what you were referring to - and I've got two of these documents for you - to illustrate that when we are talking about an army corps there are indeed different types of corps. And that two of the -- one of the qualifications that is important when looking at a corps is that if you have a heavy corps or a light corps, and if you have a heavy corps because, for example, it could be or armoured or mechanised. I would like you to confirm that an armoured corps, we are talking about a corps where most of the troops will be armoured; whereas, a mechanised corps will be most of the troops being infantry but using track vehicles. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is based on the idea of the former Warsaw Pact, vis-a-vis NATO-type corps. This is totally outdated. These two different types of army, armed and mechanised corps don't exist. It even didn't exist in my army during the time I was just talking about, because you always have a mixture of troops to give the most of flexibility to the commanding general. So you have mechanised forces even in the brigade and in the division you have already this kind of mixture. So there is only a heavy corps, which could be an armoured or mechanised, and it's always mixed, and there might be a light corps, like light infantry and air mobile. But that's basically it. And even this has been disbanded today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Maybe my question was not precise enough. What I was referring to is not how you would refer to the corps but that basically if a corps uses more armoured or mechanised, or if a corps uses -- is motorised or a light, in terms that it does not have either wheel or track vehicles, that this would have a bearing on the number of soldiers in the corps and that this will also have a bearing on the support element required for the corps to operate.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the size of the corps might be different because non-mechanised forces normally are stronger; they have more personnel than mechanised forces. But the support for mechanised forces, on the other hand, is much more exceeding this of -- of light infantry. So there is an offset. And it's very difficult to categorise like this; therefore, I'm very hesitant to say, "Yes, you are right." Because all the corps today are -- the way we do them, they are somehow structured in a very modular system, based on the mission they might have. And this is a little bit too antique -- historically too antique. It used to be more this way, but it's not any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Maybe I would just like to say, to follow on with this question: The corps you commanded had 90.000 troops, and was there a relationship because -- between the size of your corps and the type of equipment, because you had Panzer Grenadier Division, and also with the fact that because you had a Panzer Grenadier Division, which is mechanised infantry, that you needed a very large support element?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. But let me explain again. A Panzer Grenadier Division is made up of three brigades: two mechanised brigades, and an armoured brigade. But in the armoured brigade you have a mechanised battalion, and in every mechanised brigade you have at least also one armoured brigade -- battalion, so this is always a mixture right from the beginning where you mix as far down as possible. And just to show you the difference from where we are right now. In the former Bundeswehr, we used to have 5.800 tanks in the German Army. Today we are down to 530. So this is less than 10 per cent which we used to have, so we are much more turning today to a total different kind of corps. So again, this is nice for history, but this is for the last five, six years already not in existence any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the nature of the comments made by the witness regarding this document, I don't intend to produce it as an exhibit, so I should like to go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] This sketch or this document, General, again is not to put a tag on a corps but simply to illustrate that if a corps has to accomplish a mission abroad in, for example, another country, or should a corps have to do some -- some -- accomplish its mission on its own territory, there might be a difference in the size of the corps, and again in the support element required for both types of corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. But it's not only the logistic support. It's even more the command and control support which you need. If you deploy abroad, you have to build up everything from scratch. If you defend your own country, you use everything you have in your country for the well-being and the sake of your defensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to tender this document and could I have a number for it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, regarding this document, please, "Nature of military corps," any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again the Prosecution has no objection, with the caveat that this is obviously based on United States Marine Corps material, based on the text of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH137.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We can move on to the next document, Madam Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, you will have understood from my questions that what I'm trying to achieve is simply to give information to the Trial Chamber as to what is a corps and what a corps does. And would you agree with me that the document you now have in front of you is a document that outlines or highlights the different levels of war, moving from the strategic level, to the operational level, down to the tactical level, and that this really determines where a corps will fit and that the corps indeed fits in at the operational level of war?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To be a bit more precise, could you, General, elaborate a bit further in terms of the difference between the strategic level, the operational level, and the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say ten years ago the answer was rather simple because the strategic level was always all the means and efforts a country as an entire unity -- as an entire body would dispose for an operation. So it's not only the military; it's the whole economic, political, moral, and other efforts a country combines in -- in the pursuit of an objective which he would then pursue by military forces. But strategy always involves, based on -- on the definition which we have from Clausewitz, that the political and the moral and the economic things are -- are prevailing the operation -- the military operations. The operational level, until about ten years ago in my army and most other armies, were more or less contained to the corps level, but this is history. Because in out-of-area operations even a small operation of a special forces company or so could have operational consequences and is being called an operation. So the level of a -- of an organisation is not the key hinge to the question is this operational or is this tactical. The question is how important is it to pursue the strategy of this individual country. So normally the tactical level is platoon, company, battalion, brigade; division is already in -- in different ways. Some countries don't have corps any more; some countries don't have divisions, and they fight brigades by corps. So this is a little bit blurred, and you really have to look on the mission these forces have to accomplish, whether it's a tactical or an operational mission. For instance, in the last war in Iraq, a division, the 3rd Armoured Division or the 3rd Mechanised Division attacking Baghdad had an operational level. Even so, normally a division would be beyond that. But in that particular case, no question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, other than the same caveat as with respect to the previous documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, can we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... DH138.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a further document, General, I would like to show you in relation to the levels of war, to confirm basically what you have just said. Could you confirm, General, that this diagram illustrates the linkages between the strategic level, the operational level, and the tactical level?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To try and portray this diagram, which may look a bit complicated to people who have never seen diagrams like this one before, could you confirm if I create -- if I try to make it very simple that at the tactical level I will assign troops and give them a very specific task, that at the operational level the task accomplished will have a role, in terms of the campaign, and that at the strategic level all the campaign, everything that takes place at the campaign, fits in into the overall strategic objective of a state?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is a very good description of that picture -- of that flow chart. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to tender this document into evidence also, and can I have an exhibit number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, can you give us the references for this document, which is obviously an annex to another document, a book. Where was this table taken from? And you could also ask the witness whether this table applies to the NATO countries; is it applicable to the countries of the former Warsaw Treaty, though ex-Yugoslavia was not a member of the Warsaw Treaty countries, and was it applicable -- did it apply in 1993? Because judging by the responses of the witness, he appears to be referring to the situation as it is today. What is of interest to the Chamber is 1993. So does this table apply to the situation in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are quite right. I will be more specific with my questions because, of course, the aim is to assist the Chamber. So I apologise for this shortcoming on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... that this diagram does not really refer to any particular army doctrine, whether it was Warsaw Pact or NATO, but that this is more basic military principles and that they were indeed applicable in 1993 to most armies in the world, including the warring factions in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was -- I'm sorry, was this a question? I thought this was a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This was.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't have the exact source of the document. I believe that it is a part of a Canadian book. However, I can't give you the exact reference. I can provide it to you at a later stage. I would like to note, Mr. President, that on the right-hand side there is a number which is DLCD6. This refers to a Canadian book, and I can give you the exact reference at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... DH139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, maybe I was too quick. Maybe the Prosecution would like to object to this document which has been confirmed by the witness, who said that this general table was applicable to the situation that existed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President. We would be grateful once Mr. Bourgon's identified the source if that could be provided at a later date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Madam Registrar, once again could we have the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] I have a further document, General, which I would like to show to you, and this document once again deals with the levels of war, as we believe that it is important to understand at what level the war fighting was taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993. This document, General, does have references. It is taken from NATO doctrine. It is also taken from United States doctrine. And the document itself again portrays my description given a little earlier on as to what happens at the operational level of war. I draw your attention to the part in the middle from the United States where in bold it reads: "Activities at this level link tactics and strategy by establishing operational objectives needed to accomplish those strategic objectives, sequencing events to achieve the operational objectives, initiating actions and applying resources to bring about and sustain these events." Could you confirm, General, that this description of the operational level would have been an application in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a general military principle in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we talk about corps operations [Realtime transcript read in error "cooperations"], yes, sir, because the corps operations [Realtime transcript read in error "cooperations"] were the linkage between the strategic objectives of the country and -- and to transfer those, then, in operations which were accomplished on the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry to interrupt. Before my learned colleague goes on, I think there might be an error in the transcript, page 32, line 1. I'm not sure if the witness said, "If we talk about corps operations" or if he said, "We talk about cooperations." And that word is repeated twice. Perhaps my learned colleague can clear that up prior to proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can you please clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I don't know if you can read the transcript in front of you or if you -- do you have the transcript in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just tried to find it, but I definitely was talking about "corps operations" and not "cooperative operations." I was talking about the operations of the 3rd or the 5th or what have you corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I have a number for this document that I wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a further document I would like to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, the document which is -- has just been given to you illustrates the principal elements that you would find in an army. Could you confirm -- now, you see from this diagram that it comes from NATO doctrine, because at the left it talks about supreme allied headquarters. Could you confirm that normally within a state this would be the typical organisation of the army and that there would indeed be the two components in the field and at home; whereas, in the field the national army headquarters will be composed of, for example, a corps divided normally into some three divisions, but that could change. As you mentioned, it could be very flexible. And that within a division, there will be between two and four brigades, and that this will be the typical organisation of a brigade? Could you --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think what you said is right. But one has to see that there are also situations, like there were in the former German Army, before the war came down that the army in the field and the army at home were just one army. And I think this is important to mention, because this was the same application for the Bosnian forces. There were territorial forces at home and forces in the field. They -- you could not distinguish between them. So this is for expeditionary forces. But for forces defending their own country, this distinction is normally not the way you have army structured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You actually beat me to my question, because what I wanted to ask you was whether in the case of an army defending its own territory, whether you would have to overlap both these organisations and to link it into one.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender this document into evidence. I don't have the exact source. We only know that we -- that this document originates from the NATO documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President, but perhaps again if -- if the Defence is in a position perhaps in the next few days to identify the specific source of the document, we would be grateful for that. But we have no objection to the document being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Bourgon, can you please make sure that -- to tell us where this document originates from. Madam Registrar, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... DH141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] I have two documents I would like to give to the witness together, and then I would like to -- later on I would ask them to -- to introduce them as evidence as one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, could you confirm that the two documents you have just been given - they are a bit long to read, but if you can glance through these documents - the first one illustrates the corps commander's campaign design. Could you by looking at this document explain in your own words and experience what we mean -- what is meant by a "campaign design" and whether this part of a doctrine manual from Canada would illustrate the normal corps commander's campaign design and that it would have been applicable in 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's not such a big contradiction in this, because what I see from that Canadian pamphlet here, it is also very much mission-oriented; i.e., the commander gets the mission to attack or defend an objective. He's given the means to do that. But the way how he does it is up to him. So the way how he decides which forces to use, for what particular course of action within his overall campaign plan, and how he basically prioritised the mission of his forces, how he does the supporting element, and how he cooperates with the neighbouring forces, this is his intuition which he's working out with his staff, and this, then, will become a decision and out of this decision you devise a campaign plan. General Guderian was very ad libitum in this way. He was not very much reduced in his freedom of operating by the time, based on the German doctrine that they say the mission is up to the commander on the ground to execute it the best way possible without interference from higher headquarters. In other countries, you have a very different way where every different detailed step of the campaign has to be approved by higher headquarters, and then the higher headquarters controls it in a much, much more rigid way than we would do it in this German or British or French mission-oriented kind of operations. So there's a big difference in -- in the way of -- taking the initiative to react in time according to the situation as it deploys in the field. As far as I know and as far as I have deducted from the documents which I read on the JNA and my discussions with former JNA officers, their restriction in freedom of movement on the lower level in a -- in a kind of mission-oriented way of doing business was much more reduced than in the way it has been depicted here. It's a different way of coordinating operations. The one is giving more trust to the subordinate that he would do the job accordingly. And then you also have to accept that he commits mistakes [sic]. In the American Army, for instance, the -- the different orders given to the commander are much more in detail than they are in the German and in the British Army. And as far as I remember in the Warsaw Pact and as I talked also to my East German colleagues once we went together, the rigidity was much, much deeper than anything I ever encountered for the decision-making of -- on my level and on our way of doing this military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, based on the -- what is depicted in this historical perspective from General Guderian in 1940, my question to you is that what -- the issues a corps commander deals with are indeed issues such as those represented on those documents.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issues is that he basically selects the terrain in which he will fight his campaign, that he prepares the troops, prioritises the troops, the way he sees them best fit for his operation, and the whole support going with that, but all this within the framework of the overall operational objective given to him by his higher command. A corps commander has an army commander; an army commander by that time had an army group commander; and above this was the army commander, and above the army command you had Hitler. So there were quite a few echelons in between. And he had to make sure that his campaign really fit into the overall picture of the campaign, which he describes here, the proper way. So he always had to think at least two echelons above his level to make sure that everything he conceives and decides as an operational campaign really fits into the overall plan of the campaign which he was aware of, rather than only seeing his little nitty-gritty area of terrain in which he was conducting his operations. I think this is the key thing that you always transfer your ideas, your operational ideas, at least two levels higher, depending on the -- on the level in the individual state. At that time, he really had to think three levels higher in order to comply with the overall campaign plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Now, if I try to take the same information and to apply it to Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993, having a corps commander and not -- no specific corps commander, but are these the type of issues a corps commander would have been dealing with given the situation of the corps, which was, as you know, between the Supreme Command in Sarajevo and the rest of the troops down in the field? Would that be the kind of issues that would have been or should have been, in any event, on the commander's mind during the waging of war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander in Bosnia always had to take in consideration the objectives of his strategic level; i.e., the -- the supreme headquarters of his army, and also the strategic ideas his president had for the campaign, because it shows that President Izetbegovic was very keen on what was going on there, obviously, in a rather small country. So as a corps commander, I think you always had to keep in mind what were the objectives on the political level, what were the objectives on the highest military level, the Supreme Command, before you start your thinking about the own operations which were just only a means to achieve the strategic and operational objectives of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender the two documents, and can I have two numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are two documents. We have been asked to give them a number, one number. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Madam Registrar, can we have one number for these two documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... DH142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH142. We have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to show the witness the last document, which consists of two pages, and this is what I would like to finish with before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, I'm -- you have just been provided with two documents, or two pages of one document. The first document, the source is indicated at the top. Would you agree with me that if I look at the overall structure and where the corps fits in within a sovereign country and the overall hierarchy of every unit, going from a detachment all the way up to the Defence Ministry, with the figures that are provided and the rank structure that is provided, that this would more or less be the typical organisation and that what is in the frame actually shows where the corps fits in?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Bourgon, but one has to see that there are corps which don't fight divisions; they fight directly brigades. The level of the division, then, is not established in this particular army, which applies more often than one would believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I try to follow up on your answer -- if I try to follow up: In the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were not officially any divisions; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, would this be, taking into account the numbers might be a bit higher on this sketch than what you would find in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would that illustrate basically and give an understanding of someone to know the hierarchy of the units and approximate numbers and the relationship between the various units?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move to the second page, which is really -- again, we have the reference to this document -- and that is to really put it into a very easy and common definition, in terms of being -- that the corps headquarters -- sorry, I look at the middle paragraph: "A corps consists of a corps headquarters, corps troops, and such divisions as may be assigned to it." And if I look on top of the corps, you will find the headquarters, which is above, and then: "The corps headquarters is designed so that a single commander can coordinate the combat operations of two or more divisions." Would that be a very common but easy representation of where and what a military corps does?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But again, division is not a must. It could be an operational group; it could be nothing. It could be that the division level is deleted and instead of division then you would have a brigade, and the brigade would be directly under the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I apply this to Bosnia and Herzegovina more specifically --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I have a number for this document. And this is actually the last part of my examination -- cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... DH143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have arrived at the break time. It is half past 10.00. And we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will continue, Mr. President, with the second part of my cross-examination, that is, questions regarding the concepts of command which, we believe, could be useful to the Chamber in their determinations. And it will also allow us to check and confirm above all the ability of the witness to assist the Chamber as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General Reinhardt, we ended up with -- before the break by going through one of -- a sketch which illustrates the typical organisation of a corps. Are you familiar, General, with a concept known as span of control?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you give your own definition, based on your own knowledge, of what is meant by span of control.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The span of control basically encompasses the variety of units you can coordinate and control in an effective way if you have too many subordinate units or subunits, it's very difficult to control in detail what they are doing. So there's only a certain number which normally should be controlled from a higher headquarters. And this is basically a question of the organisation of the individual army, how they do this, and what you just told us is reflecting a span of control that on all different levels you have somebody who really can have a grip of what's going on on the subordinate level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to show you a document which is taken from Canadian doctrine and also from Harvard Business School concerning span of control. General, I refer to you in terms of the top of this document, where it is mentioned, paragraph 3, "span of control," which basically highlights exactly what you just said, in terms of: "There is a limit to how much one person can effectively direct. A formation, or units, number of subordinate activities, and its air of operations must be such that one person can command or control the formation or unit." Do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the middle paragraph, taken from the Harvard Business Review of 1956; there's a paragraph basically that says at the end, and I'll just read the highlighted or the portion in bold: "If you have too many people reporting to you, two things will happen, both bad. First, you will become the organisation's bottleneck and can quickly blow away any money you save by getting rid of middle management; second, it becomes much harder for the individuals reporting to you to feel that their work is seen, recognised, and appreciated." Could you give or state whether this paragraph can have a military application.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what I said before. Therefore, you have individual levels in between which help you to execute command and control, not directly but with having other people sharing your span of control on the lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as to the third part of this document, which is basically a quote from, I take it, some -- General, Sir Ian Hamilton, and I refer to the last part of this group, where it says: "Organisations are run by rule, a rule whereby from three to six hands are shepherded by one head, each head in turn being a member of a superior group of from three to six who are being wielded into line one by one. And as to whether the groups are three, four, five, or six, it is useful to bear in mind a by-law." And this is what I would like to ask your opinion on, this by-law: "The smaller the responsibility of the group member, the larger may be the number of group -- of the group and vice versa; that is to say, one NCO..." which I take to stand for non-commissioned officer, "...in charge of three private soldiers would be too idle; however, one lieutenant general in charge of six divisional generals would be too busy." Could you say whether you agree with this statement.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what it means to bear in mind a by-law. I don't understand this term. But the basic content of this paragraph is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to tender this document into evidence. It comes from the Canadian doctrine, on top; the middle part comes from the Harvard Business Review; and the third part from a book by Sir Ian Hamilton, "The Soul and Body of an Army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Registrar, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH144.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To move on this with document, General, talking about span of control, would you say that a commanding general taking steps to reduce his span of control or, to be more precise, to increase and enhance his command and control takes steps to reduce the number of immediate subordinates that will report to him in order to be more effective? Would you call such a commander a reasonable commander, or how would you qualify such a commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a clever commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me go on, General, by showing you another document. This document, General, is the basic organisation of a corps. What I would like to ask you, General, on this specific diagram is to confirm whether the corps depicted on this diagram, which is in fact a true corps, which is the 5th US Corps, which is normally stationed in Germany and presently deployed in Iraq and which includes 42.000 troops, is that -- could you recognise the contents of this corps, based on your knowledge, and whether this would be an organisation of a corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And it used to be one of my corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In respect of this specific corps, General, I note at the bottom of the diagram where we have a mention of the 13th Panzer Grenadier Division, which is stationed in Germany but not included in the total strength. Based on your knowledge, can you say exactly or more -- with more details what was the relationship between the 5th US Corps, from the United States, and the 13th Panzer Grenadier Division from Germany?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rather simple relation. In peacetime, the 13th Panzer Grenadier Division is a pure German division. In case of war, i.e., defence of NATO, the 13th Panzer Grenadier Division becomes an organic part of the 5th US Corps, which is a US/German corps. So the 13th Panzer Grenadier Division in its training, in its command and control, as far as war is concerned, is an entirely integrated part of the 5th US/German Corps.
