utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to tender this document as an illustration of a typical corps according to the standards of NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH145.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, you mentioned a little earlier in answer to one of my questions looking at your -- or reviewing your qualifications that the staff officers assigned at the corps headquarters were the best amongst the professional officers and that you would always get the best at the corps headquarters. You would get fully professional and qualified officers. Is that a fair recap of what you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that in order for a corps commander such as yourself, when you commanded three corps in Germany, that it is very important for a corps commander, of course any commander but even more so for a corps commander, to rely on a very effective staff?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is key. The commander is only as good as his staff is, so the better the staff, the more competent the commander could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a diagram of the general staff assigned to corps headquarters, and I would like you to confirm that this is the type of people that would be found into a corps headquarters. Looking at this diagram, General, can you confirm that this would be a typical organisation of a corps headquarters, going from, of course, the deputy commander, down to the Chief of Staff, down to the principal advisors? And the Trial Chamber has had the opportunity to hear this, I believe, once before, but I would like you to explain what is meant by the acronyms "G1" to "G6." And also, if you can say a word about the special staff that you would find in a corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: G1 to G6, or very often also J1 to J6 if you have a joint staff, is just the abbreviation. 1 is for personnel; 2 is for intelligence; 3 is for training and operations; 4 is always wherever you are in NATO logistics; 5 is civil affairs; 6 is communications. Today we also have 7 for training; and 9 for CIMIC. So these are the normal subdivisions of the corps staff. The special staff which you see here is a very typical American special staff, which is in many ways different from other corps staff. He is very heavy on additional personnel. But normally you're sure you will have -- you will have a public relations officer, you will have a personal staff helping you to go through all the things, and you will have a staff -- a judge advocate on your staff taking care of all the legal things. So I think this is -- these are the things which you would normally have in every staff. The other things are very much Americanised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to -- you mentioned the staff judge advocate. I have a specific question unrelated to this specific diagram, but can you confirm that in the German military a staff judge advocate or a legal advisor is only found, at least in 1993, at the division level and up?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which would mean that at the brigade level, you would not in the German Army have a legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And could you comment or could you agree with me that an army which deploys legal advisors at the brigade level, or at least endeavours to do so, is an army that is very conscious about legal matters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to add on before you explained on that that our brigades deploying, for instance, to Kosovo or so, they have legal advisor because the legal business in your deployment is so paramount and takes so much precedence over other things, that without the legal advisor a brigade commander just cannot do his job in another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as to my earlier statement that an army who endeavours to deploy legal advisors, would you say that this is a conscious army about legal matters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move back to this specific diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Mr. President, I should like to tender this document, and could I have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH146.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, I have a few questions also in relation to the staff under the corps commander. Can you confirm that the Chief of Staff who manages the work -- is the one who manages the work of all the principal advisors, G1 to G6 or even to G9, as you mentioned, and that basically he is one who is in command of the headquarter element?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff is the right and the left hand of the commander. He is the most important figure after the commander. And as you said, he is coordinating the staff and the entire staff work, and he is the closest -- the closest advisor to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, to give you a specific scenario, should a commander not be available for a long period and should you have the Chief of Staff be asked to replace the commander for a long period of time, would you say that this would be extremely difficult for such a Chief of Staff in that he would have to have two positions at the same time at that moment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult, because he is overburdened by taking command responsibility plus his coordinating responsibilities as the Chief of Staff, but nevertheless this is common practice, and we expect normally that a officer who made it up through the Chief of Staff is capable of doing that for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that the aim would be to, as soon as possible, either appoint the Chief of Staff and assign him as commander or at least appoint a new commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very sensible to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As far as the deputy commander goes, General, would you agree with me that sometimes you have a deputy commander, sometimes you don't have a deputy commander, but normally the commander will decide on the duties he will assign to his deputy commander and that the deputy commander may be called upon to assume command, to replace the commander if he either gets killed or simply is not available?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Under normal circumstances, at a certain level you should have a deputy just for the case if the commander is killed or ineffective, to do his job, that another guy can take over fresh. He knows what's going on in that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Looking at -- or on the basis of your own experience, if a corps commander uses his deputy to handle many matters on the ground and to basically act -- or to have the function of his eyes on the ground, to report to him what is going on in order to be fully aware of the situation, would you -- how would you qualify such use of a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy commander in this regard is the alter ego of the commander, and he is his eyes and brains on the spot, so there's a close relation between the commander and his deputy, and everything the deputy does he does only for or on behalf of his commander. As I said, he is the alter ego of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And unless a commander has any information or specific information to the contrary, would you say that it is of the ultimate importance that he trusts his deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If he doesn't trust him, this deputy commander cannot be his alter ego, so there must be a very close relation. And I assume that the deputy commander, everything he has done or does is in very close or closest coordination with his commander and the commander knows what the deputy has done and why he has done what he has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if a commander assigns a mission to his deputy commander and upon return to the headquarters the deputy commander informs the commander of how the mission was accomplished and the result of that mission, would it be normal for the commander to fully trust the information he is provided with?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on, General, to the issue of communications which was raised in your report, in terms of the importance of communications. Would you agree with me, General, that to operate effectively the corps commander must be supported by an effective system of communications which will link all military formations and that the aim of this is to allow him to receive reports and returns from subordinate units and also to transmit reports and returns to his superior headquarters at the army level?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that SOPs, or standard operating procedures, related to communications facilitate and standardise communications between all military units?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These SOPs basically standardise the way the content should be broken down, so everybody knows where he's report -- where he's supposed to report. But also the time when a message is due and what the contents of the message should be all about. This goes in -- in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that a commander who does issue instructions to his lower formation or lower units, subordinate units, sorry, in terms of how and when and concerning what issues they are to report to him, that this is indeed part of the corps commander's functions?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of his functions, and this is the daily routine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you say that a commander who does issue such SOPs is indeed doing his job properly?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned in your report and again yesterday that the superior headquarters was responsible for setting up the communications system which will link it to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this -- am I right in saying that this refers to the putting in place of the communications system?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once that system is in place, could you confirm - and I'd like to give you a specific example - if a subordinate unit changes location, can you confirm that it will be the subordinate unit's responsibility to re-establish links with the superior headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a yes or no answer I can give you to that. The subordinate unit will change the location and report this immediately to higher headquarters, but very often the receiving end of higher headquarters at that subordinate headquarters -- I mean the receiving end in communications basically moves with the subordinate command at the same time, so it's also their mission to report to their signal brigade of the corps, for instance, that they have moved with this particular brigade. So it's a twofold thing which shows the responsibility. One is the technical responsibility; we have moved to another headquarters. And the other one is the communication responsibility, of those communication means provided by higher headquarters, that the higher headquarters knows that they have moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I ask you to comment on simply common sense and your expertise that it would be normal for the lower -- the lower or the subordinate unit to know where the superior headquarters is located but that the opposite might not always be true?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might be the case. Even I cannot imagine that. But under normal conditions, I would say the superior headquarters knows where its subordinate headquarters are deployed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in a combat environment, when issue -- when orders have been issued and that the area in which this subordinate headquarters is conducting its operations, the superior headquarters will know the general area where its subordinate unit is but might not know the exact location within that area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might be. And again, that depends very much on the level we are talking about, sir. If we talk about the battalion, it might be that the battalion doesn't know for a certain period of time where a specific company is doing its operations and the company might not know where every individual platoon is. But having a rather static headquarters on the brigade level and a rather static headquarters on the corps level, I would assume that on this level you normally would know where your counterpart is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, the -- you mentioned that communications could be established in many ways, and I think you did mention - but correct me if I'm wrong - that communications could be established by courier, which is the most direct and simple form of communication, radio, telephone, satellite, electronic - and I have another note, but I can't even read my own handwriting, I'm sorry - but would you agree with me that there are many ways in which communications can be established and maintained?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think in addition to what you just said today, very often it's email, the computer system as such, plus Motorola. Motorola basically today is -- is superseding almost every other means of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that a corps commander who uses all the means at his disposal is a reasonable commander who is trying to do the best -- his best in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the section that we're dealing with today is most -- for the most part simply information and knowledge. And as you could see, I have some specific questions, but tomorrow I will move into the specifics. But with this particular issue, based on the documents that you have seen, can you confirm that the corps commander in this case went out of his way to establish communication with the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did the utmost to establish and to keep this communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One last question dealing with communications, General: Would it be normal for a military unit, a subordinate unit, which is not able to communicate with the superior headquarters, to try and establish or re-establish the communications link by doing what is called a relay and going by -- through another unit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a must, and this is also normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Based on the documents that you have reviewed, have you seen any instances where subordinate units have had to use the relay technique, because they could not reach their superior headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I have seen one, but I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the documents that you have seen, General - and this will be my last specific question, because this is not the aim of my questions today - did you see documents or orders or reports in which subordinate units were complaining about the lack of effective communications within the corps area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. There is a report of the 3rd Corps complaining about the poor communications on the tactical level, and there are reports of the operational group, the Operational Group Bosanska Krajina, but there are also reports of the 7th Mountain Brigade -- motorised -- the 7th Mountain Brigade -- Muslim Mountain Brigade, complaining about the poor communication means and the way how they tried -- how they tried to overcome that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I'd like to show you one document in order to finish with the issue of the way a corps controls its information. This document, General, is -- portrays typical distances or area of responsibility of a corps, and it is quoted as being: "An example of the parameters for a defensive operation." According to what we see on the diagram, the area of interest would be 300 kilometres; the area of influence would be 150 kilometres; whereas, the front line will be anywhere from 30 to -- to 80 kilometres. Looking at page 2, the terms, "area of responsibility," "area of interest," and "area of influence" are defined. Can you, by looking at this document, and in your own -- based on your own professional experience confirm that these would be typical figures for a corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the figures which you get out of the manuals. But again, as I have said before, a corps is very much composed on the mission - and it's a modular system - and the question is: What means does the corps have to effectively influence the battle? If you have a normal standard corps like a German corps with an artillery range of about 30 kilometres maximum, it's no use that you extend this if you cannot influence the area for which you are responsible. An American corps, which has with the -- with the modern MLRS system a range of influencing what's going on on the battle up to 350 kilometres, the operational depth is totally different. So really you have to see this as a normal parameter, which you then have to adopt to the capabilities of your original corps, how to influence the area of influence, how you can react in there, and also how broad your -- your area of responsibility is at the beginning. So these are figures of the thumb which have to be adapted to the real capabilities of -- of the individual corps which is in that area. I just want to make that caveat, because otherwise these numbers might stick. They are only rough rules of the thumb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If I move more specifically to the frontage or the -- the size of the front line, would you agree with me that the longer your front line is, the more difficult it will be on the corps itself but also on the planning of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me that should that front line be two different front lines with two different enemies, that that would make things even more complicated on the corps and more complicated on the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a hell of a difficult job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me, General, that -- I refer to the last sentence of the bottom of page 1, where it says that: "The corps commander usually plans up to 96 hours ahead."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you explain what this means in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the brigade commander and the division commander fighting the actual battle on the ground, and the corps commander is influencing this battle by attaching additional means, cross-attaching forces, but besides that he keeps out of the actual battle -- this is not his business. He plans and has his hat free for the things which might follow on, and he has to think much farther in advance because the cooperation with the air force, the movement of troops in order to influence the battle in three, four, five days in order to establish the support accordingly to the follow-on operation takes time. It normally takes much more time than we anticipate, and therefore it's his business not to be bogged down with what's going on right now but to look into the future, to imagine what might happen on his level, on the side of the enemy, and to take the appropriate measures in order that they can be executed in time, that after 96 hours they are effective on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would this commentary apply to a corps commander in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think seeing the -- the operations as they have been conducted - and these are operations not on the very large scale; these are many, many small-scale operations which had to be planned and operated upon - I think the duration of the planning staff of a corps in Bosnia-Herzegovina might have been shorter than 96 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How much shorter? Half? Three-quarters? What?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't want to give a figure, because the distances were much smaller. He had to fight with the forces available. They were not so large distances as you would normally have when the corps moving large units from one area to the next one. The cooperation with the air force was not the key issue, which normally is one of the key problems for a corps headquarters, where you always have to think in three to four days in advance because there was no Bosnian air force really supporting the land forces. So the -- the elements the corps commander had to deal with, the problems he had to deal with were much closer to him and to his staff than it would normally be to a corps staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, tomorrow I will show you two specific operations that were planned, and then we can again come back on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment I would like to tender the document into evidence, and may I have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document about the responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objection to this document. We would, however, as with the two previous documents, ask that the Defence could please provide us with a source when they have that information available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Registrar, may we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH147. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is going to provide the Prosecution with the source of the document as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Let me move on, General, by going through the responsibilities and the operations as a corps, depending on the type of military assignment it is involved in. I will try to move a bit quicker, but I'd like to propose to you that there are some basic missions that can be assigned to a corps. I'll give you six examples, and I would like if you can confirm whether these are six typical examples of assignments which can be given to a corps in any country. These six examples are as follows: The first one is a corps involved in support to civil power; for example, in a course of disaster relief. Is that a typical assignment of a corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be an assignment, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second type would be in support to civil authority; for example, in a case of internal disturbances, to assist in the maintenance of law and order.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, but in many countries it's forbidden. In my country, it's absolutely impossible to talk about this. And we're just having a big discussion in Germany. It's not possible in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in other NATO countries it's not possible either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know of any countries where this is indeed possible?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's -- if I see that correctly, it's possible, for instance, in France, where they even have special forces to do this, "Les Gendarmerie." It's possible in Italy where they also have special forces to do this, like the "Carbonari." And where the constitution is different. Our constitution is very much based on the history of our country, and therefore many things are not allowed to the German military which are allowed in other countries. Like also in the United States it's possible; you can call up the National Guard and use it for antiriot, which is absolutely impossible in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The other type of assignment could be, for example, a peacekeeping mission, such as UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Another possible assignment would be a peace enforcement mission, such as IFOR, or the implementation force in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Another possible assignment would be to wage war in another country.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a sixth -- another possible assignment could be to wage war on its own national territory.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I compare the six different assignments - there might be others - but if I compare the six I've highlighted to you, would you agree that the toughest assignment, the most difficult and the most complex assignment that can be given to a corps is to wage war on its own national territory when it is being attacked?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably the most important one and a very difficult one to execute. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I compare these six types of assignments, would you agree with me, General, that the legal regime applicable to each is likely to be different?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I give you, for example, that in disaster-relief assistance, most likely national law would apply plus maybe some specific legislation.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In aid to civil authority, which you say does not exist or could not exist in Germany, then it would be national law for sure where it exists.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the army would definitely be subordinate to civil authorities.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In a peacekeeping mode, the law that would apply is likely to be United Nations Charter Chapter 6.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plus the laws of the individual nations which have deployed forces, because the national law for the soldiers operating abroad applies to them even abroad, and that makes the thing so complicated. Because the national laws are so -- in many ways so different from country to country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as far as international law goes - I'm not sure whether you'll be able to answer this question or if you know based on your experience - but even though it might not apply officially because it might not be specifically in force, the troops who participate in peacekeeping mission will always be asked by their own country as a minimum to apply the spirit and principles of international law, such as the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we move into the peace enforcement assignment, then the legal regime would be the United Nations Chapter 7, which allows for the use of force to accomplish the mandate.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in addition, as you've mentioned, national law and international law.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we move into waging war into another country, you will agree with me that the only possibility of doing so legally would be to do so under collective self-defence, which is United Nations Charter Article 51, where you come to the help of another country, and that in such a case international law applies and the full body of international humanitarian law applies?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right. But the interpretation of Charter -- Article 51 of the United Nations charter is pretty broad. This is one of the problems which we are realising right now. I understand what you're saying. I agree to that, but there are nations who see that differently, or their -- their interpretation of Article 51 is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And in the last type of assignment I referred to, which is waging war on your own national territory, this is likely, at least if the attack is coming from another state, this is likely to be in self-defence mode, again under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, but at the same time would you agree with me that national laws will continue to apply, the international law will apply, and international humanitarian law will also apply, albeit it could be in a limited way, depending if it is an internal or an international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that based on this legal regime applicable when you wage war on your own territory, that the conflict of laws between national laws and international law makes it a very difficult situation, from a legal perspective?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I would like to follow you on that, because the national law and the international law are not exclusive. They are basically supplementary in many ways. And I think even if you are in a national disaster situation and defending your country, the international law and the humanitarian law has to be applied the same way as otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And these laws would have to be applied in a complimentary way.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's the way to put it. I'm sorry for my English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in conclusion on this issue, General, as to the sharing of responsibilities between the military and the civil authorities in the last scenario we covered --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- would you agree that this will depend -- that this will have, sorry, a direct bearing on the role, the functions, and the obligations of the corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I give you an example of a corps which is fighting while the civil authorities, such as the police or civil security or the courts are functioning, that this will determine and set the right and left boundaries of what the mission of the corps is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To use another example which -- of which you are familiar with, that of Kosovo. In Kosovo, you had, of course, KFOR, the international peacekeeping force of which you were the commander, and you had the United Nations Mission in Kosovo, UNMIK, and that the two shared the responsibilities for the governing of this kind of UN state, if I may use this term.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In fact, I've had the opportunity to read many of your press releases while you were commander of KFOR, in which you actually were acting along with Bernard Kouchner, and you referred to as being twin brothers taking care of the land. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to another section of my cross-examination, which deals with something you raised in your report, which is professionalism and a professional army. In this respect, would you agree with me, General, that a professional army will be one that is one, first of all, loyal to the state; and two, that will be disciplined?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one has to assume this. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that these are the two most important qualification or qualifiers which will make an army a professional army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's also the way an army has been trained. How well trained they are professionally, in consonance with the objectives of their country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at the importance of -- or the loyalty to the state, would I be right in saying that an army which is loyal to the state, it is important for at least two reasons, including that the army will have legitimate authority and that the army will have -- and that military operations will be legal?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I move on to discipline -- you did mention a lot about discipline yesterday -- would you agree that discipline refers to two things: First, discipline refers to the culture of obedience?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if you do not have discipline, it is simply not possible to have a professional army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discipline and professional army are almost synonym. But I would go one step further: A draft army is also placed on discipline, so this is not exclusively only for a professional army. It also applies to most every kind of army I can imagine, because without discipline, an army is not capable to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And discipline also refers to, General, and if you need discipline, you also have -- you also need the means to enforce, to ensure that you have a disciplined army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this has a direct bearing on your combat potential.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that a commander should as a priority focus on the discipline of his troops to ensure that he has fighting-capable troops.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is the priority, as I understand you just put it, but it's a very high priority for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When we talk about the enforcement of discipline, General, would you agree with me that what matters is that soldiers abide with the law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what they did wrong or how you qualify what they did wrong is secondary?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you qualify -- would you agree that if you want to enforce discipline, whether it is a minor disciplinary offence, such as not reporting for duty, or a criminal offence, such as stealing, that in the eyes of the commander both are important and both need to be handled?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because what the commander wants is troops that will be disciplined and that will abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: An issue has been raised in this trial - and I need -- I would like to have your opinion - and that is the issue of war crimes. You would agree with me that the same applies, whether it's a war crime, whether it's a criminal act, whether it's a disciplinary offence, they all deserve and must get the commander's attention?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because what the commander wants is to be sure that his troops are ready to fight.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Because war crimes affect the discipline considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as a matter of fact, if -- could you confirm that in Germany in 1993 it would not even have been possible for someone to be accused of a war crime because there was no such thing in German law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no war crime; there is only crime, criminal activities which then would be brought in front of a civil court. But you are right; there is no special war -- military justice in this regard, and therefore the term "war crime" in this regard is only considered against international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my understanding, General, is that this has changed with the ratification by Germany of the Statute of the International Criminal Court and that now in German law you have something called war crimes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I referred to an example that I would like to give you where in a trial before the Bavarian High Court in February of 1997 the defendant was charged with the following: Genocide, murder, and deprivation of liberty, according to Sections 221, 220A, and 239 of the German Penal Code, which defines those crimes. And this would go to show that genocide is an offence that exists or existed in 1993 in German law but that the other offences did not exist under the heading "war crimes" but existed under the heading "deprivation of liberty or murder," which could be used for any civilian or anyone.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant before. It's in the penal law which is applicable then also to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what matters again to the commander is that to ensure that any criminal act is looked upon.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I -- this is a commentary I have, and I don't want to -- to put it for the record, but I'd just like to -- it's a document that was -- it's a German document which deals with the customary law provisions of additional Protocol I. But talking about this specific trial in the Bavarian High Court, they say that both courts considered these acts as being unlawful behaviour in war, even though they were criminal acts in the German Penal Code. You can relate to this issue.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to other qualifications required for a professional army. And I would talk to you -- I would suggest to you that integrity is also a very important qualification of a professional soldier and a professional army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would suggest to you that integrity is important because integrity is mutual trust amongst soldiers but also within the chain of command and because the chain of command must be able to rely on the information it gets.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I give you an example of something that happened in Kosovo, where there were some allegations while you were commander of the force over there that Lieutenant General -- I'm not sure if I pronounce the name right, but I would try Ceku. I'm not sure if that's the right pronunciation. There were some allegations that he was responsible for violations of international law and that the matter was reported to you. Do you recall this or --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, my question is: Your answer in a -- in a press release was that there were no such surveillance -- violation and that you fully trusted Lieutenant General Ceku to have provided you with accurate information as to what had happened.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were two things I had to consider. One was that there was the accusation against Ceku, without any evidence; the other thing, this was that I had Madam Carla Del Ponte in Kosovo at almost the same time with some of her gentlemen, and I asked her whether she has anything on Ceku, and I said, "If you have anything on Ceku, I have to know that, because he's one of the key figureheads for this province, and if there's something we have to consider, then we might also reconsider his position for the Kosovo Protection Corps as a civil organisation." And I was told that there was nothing against him. So this was the reason why I then went to the press and said, "As long as I have no evidence, as long as there is no official accusation, only what is in the paper, Lieutenant General Ceku for me is still a trustworthy man."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, General, that Lieutenant General Ceku was the former head of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the UCK. He was before that a brigade commander of Croatian forces fighting in the Krajina. And he was a JNA officer, been trained there, and he was very proud of his training in the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that you assigned him, I guess -- I understand that you did assign him as commander of the Kosovo Protection Corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is wrong. Because the assignation was done, Bernard Kouchner, and he was not under my command, he was as -- the protection corps under the command and being paid by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the circumstances, the issue I would like to raise with you is that regardless of the past of Lieutenant General Ceku, regardless of the circumstances, you had dealings with him and you trusted the information that he provided you with.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because it was your understanding that as commander of the Kosovo Protection Corps he was worthy of that position and unless you get information specifically to the contrary, you would continue to trust him.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called him a couple of times on -- on accidents, on allegations in the country, even during the night, and get him in to check myself whether they were true or not, and some of these actions led to the ouster of subordinate commands of Ceku out of the Protection Corps because I said I cannot trust these guys, and I just threw them out, which was not very easy by that time, with the consequences. But I had no reason not to trust General Ceku at that time during my period, and I think he was really trying to make the utmost out of his position. And one also has to see that he is a figurehead amongst the Kosovars with probably the highest reputation of all the Kosavars in country because the people -- the Kosovo population thinks very highly of him. So if you do something against him, you really have to have hard evidence; otherwise, you have the whole population against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And my point really on this issue is that -- can you confirm the importance for a commander once he has assigned people to positions, once he is working with people subordinate to him, that it is important for him to trust these persons and to trust the information he gets from them unless he has information specifically to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. But I'd like to repeat: General Ceku was not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. General, I move on to another qualification of a professional army, and that could be volunteerism, the fact that a professional army usually will be an army of volunteers who are, one, ready to make the ultimate sacrifice of their life; and two, they are willing to pursue some kind of a career in this army, not matter at what level and what officer or non-officer?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you also agree that one of the qualifications of a professional army, and you referred to it a little earlier, would be knowledge and training?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that knowledge and training is divided into two parts: Individual training and collective training? And that this is indeed very important for a professional army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we think about training to prepare for combat or to prepare for any mission, any military assignment, a lot of care and a lot of attention will be devoted to ensuring that the soldiers are ready for whatever mission they are about to undertake.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a diagram which refers to the type of training, or at least which depicts the training cycle in preparation for a mission. This diagram comes from a Canadian military manual, and basically it highlights seven levels of training, where you will try or begin by individual battle skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am missing one copy. I'm one copy short.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could a copy be placed on the ELMO of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That level 1 of such training will begin by individual skills and battle tasks, to be followed by section training, subunit, platoon level, and then company level, and then a combat team, which means usually a mix of subunits, combat arms unit training at the battalion or even -- sorry, at the battalion level; to be followed by formation level at the brigade level. And if we look at the drawing at the bottom, this is basically the type of training, and it shows the cycle, going from at the bottom left individual training, right up to in-theatre training, and then the force is deployed. And the reconstitution phase is where you take the same soldiers following their deployment and you prepare them either for another tour of the same mission or you train them anew with a completely different training programme for a different mission. Is that the normal planning or training cycle that is used in the military to ensure that troops are ready for their deployment and their mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the almost ideal way to do that, but it doesn't say that all the nations do it like this. Very few nations do like the Canadians do. A formation-level training on the brigade level almost never happens because all the brigades are multinational today and that means that the training remains in national hands so the nations at their utmost do a battalion training. And as far as I know, with, so to speak, my Canadian battalions, Princess Patricia and Van Doos and so on, it all was on the battalion level. But, Your Honour, if I might add one point which I think is very important: Training is not just the normal military skills. A key thing in this kind of preparation for deployment is the preparation of the soldiers for the cultural, the religious, the political background on which they are forcing and to prepare them mentally, also very much on the legal level - at least, that's what most of the European nations do - so the soldiers know how important, especially this kind of non-grippable information and training is all about. And it's sometimes more important than the training with a rifle or the tank or so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. One last question concerning the qualifications of a professional army, which you referred to in your report, is experience and having an institutional background or foundation --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- based on lessons learns, on specialised training, and on a career pattern. I'm not sure these are all things you mention, but can you elaborate on this as being an important aspect of a professional army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think the ones who join a professional army want to qualify, to go up in -- in the system. And to qualify, you have to go through specific training; you have to get experience on certain levels; and you have to show that your experience on that level as a competent commander, platoon commander, battalion commander was really a solid one, a good one. Otherwise, you don't raise up through the system. So training, competence goes very closely with your career. If you don't qualify adequately, you won't make it. And I think it's the inherent desire of a professional soldier that he doesn't stay on the lowest level but he wants to proceed as far as he can go, and his career is very much affected by his capabilities and his professional knowledge in -- in the way he can prove it -- the best way he can prove is in the staffs and in the command functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you -- would you agree with me that the last two issues we covered, knowledge and training, as well as experience and having a force with an institutional background, that all of this, if you do not have this prior to being thrown into combat, that this can be very difficult?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I was very clear on this in my statement, making sure that everybody understands how difficult it was for the Bosnian forces to build up their forces under those very adverse conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that - and I give you a hypothetical scenario - that if in such circumstances a corps commander would nevertheless attempt to train his troops, both individual training and also collective training, and even officer training at the command level, that such a commanding general would be a very reasonable commander with -- doing more than his best in the circumstances at the time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be very reasonable because without doing that, it would be even more difficult for him to have forces available to operate with them according to the mission given to him. So it's in his own interest, in his own professional interest to do exactly what you just said. The more you raise the level of your forces, the more effective your forces will be to do what they're supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the last question on this is: To mix training while you're fighting a war, to mix the two, is indeed something very difficult.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You only can use the pauses in the operations to train the soldiers and to apply what they have learned in combat in order to reinforce this knowledge, but it is very, very difficult, but it can be done to some extent. And it's been done to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to tender this document. I have one more topic to address before the break. I don't know when we are going to take the break, but I have just one more topic. I should now like to have a -- an exhibit number for this document on training and education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, the last issue I would like to cover before the break -- again, I say "technical break"; it's not because we want to take a break - but it's the creation of a professional army. Would you agree with me that to create a professional army requires many things. And I will suggest to you some of the things that are required to create a professional army. The first thing is you would need governmental legality and governmental legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second thing would be: There would have, of course, to be a raison d'etre and a plan to create an army which normally will be based on the need for security of a sovereign nation.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree to that. It's not necessary to build up an army because the nation is under threat, but the part of the sovereignty, the self-esteem of a country, a sovereign country, basically requires it to have its own forces for self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Another thing that would be required to build a professional army would be time.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It takes a lot of time to build a professional force.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally it takes much more time than people anticipate, and we see this right now in reality how difficult it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Some people have even suggested that by the time an army is a fully professional army, it may take as much as 30 years; whereas, your first recruits have reached the top of your army. Now, even though this would probably be the -- the higher end of the spectrum, would you agree with such a statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it takes a lot of time, but I wouldn't quote any -- any specific years' time, because it's always very, very dependent on the circumstances under which you build up an army. And let me -- let me refer to the one we are discussing on -- on Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were officers who have been already in the training who have been experienced and professional officers in the Yugoslav army who could transfer this information and their training to their soldiers, so they started very, very cold from scratch. Otherwise, we have the wrong impression here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I was just leading to that -- coming to that question concerning human resources. Of course, if you want to build an area of responsibility, you need human resources. And as much as possible, you also need qualified human resources.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And by "qualified" I mean to make a soldier it takes training and almost any human being but if you need a doctor, if you need engineers, and if you need lawyers, then if you have such professional qualification as raw material, then you use those and go faster.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also need, of course, material resources, where to build an army takes a lot of money, because you need weapons, you need vehicles, and you need infrastructures.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to build an army, you also right from the get-go must include an individual training system, as well as a professional education and development system.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if you put all of these together, then you will be able to create a professional army with time.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that today it would be quicker to build a professional army because we have computers and because we have some kind of collective memory, we can go on the Internet, like I said, and pick all these document manuals. So it is possible to go quicker, based on more information being available today. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Even if you have all this information available, you have to transfer this information into the knowledge of the individual soldier. So the transformation process from having the knowledge here and getting it into the behaviour of the soldier hasn't changed, no matter how much information is applicable by that time. So they -- the time to need -- you need for the transformation of a civilian into a good soldier is unaffected by our modern information age.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One example I'd like to give you concerning procurement, because you have been involved in procurement: It has been suggested that for a nation to buy a tank, from the moment the requirement is identified, from the moment the tank is delivered to the squadron, it could be up to ten years.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very optimistic. I think it never happens in that short period of time, at least not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, to do all of this, General, the creation of a professional army with all these requirements and to have to do this and to try and put it into perspective, with a 5 per cent of the troops being already professional troops but 95 per cent of the troops being untrained soldiers or former conscripts, would you agree with me that this would be a very difficult challenge to do so in a combat environment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt about this, but I don't want to take an untrained soldier on the same level as a conscript soldier. If you have a good conscript system, the conscript soldiers still know a lot about what they have learned, and you will use them to the utmost. And to come one step back, you don't have to reinvent the wheel every time; you can buy things or use things which you find on the market and don't develop it on your own, because otherwise you will really need the 30 years, as you said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, a commanding general who is fighting a war on his own national territory in a defensive mode, being attacked by two enemies, trying to create an army, trying to develop a training system, being bogged down by some communications problem, how would you describe this type of situation for a commanding general and what would be his focus at the time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must be a world champion in improvisation. And there is not only one focus; there is a whole bunch of focuses he has to concentrate his efforts, because the key thing is for him to do the defence of his country against those who attack him. And everything he does has to be focussed on -- on this objective, and this is such a variety that I just -- I just hesitate to say that there is one focus only. This is just not possible, to focus on one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have another topic for the rest of the day dealing with the responsibilities of a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is 12.25. We will resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General Reinhardt, I'd like to move on with the cross-examination on the responsibilities of a corps commander, of a commanding general. I would like before I do so, however, to show you two more documents. I would like to have the usher show these documents to the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If there are documents left over, if we can bring them to the interpreters. I forgot to bring it to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, it would be very useful for the interpreters to put all the documents on the ELMO, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, I ask you to take a look at, first of all, the document which has a diagram called Figure 2.1, "Combat power." And I would ask if you can put it on the ELMO, which is the device immediately to your right. And this will allow everyone to see the diagram. This, General Reinhardt, is a Canadian document that relates to combat power. The aim of the Defence in producing this document or in showing it to you is whether you can relate moving from the centre, where you have the commander in the middle, or the function of command, and where you have combat power being defined into two distinct circles, the first one meaning the combat functions, as being the main effort, the tempo of operations, and synchronisation; and followed by, in the inner circle, the six combat functions, as being command, followed by information operations, followed by manoeuvre, firepower, protection, and sustainment. I am not so much interested as -- in the text that I'm presenting to you, but could you relate that this diagram does represent the way we can picture combat operations and how you can increase your combat power by following this procedure.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can increase your combat power, but you can maximise it in a way, because you don't get anything in addition to what you have right now. Therefore, "increase" is probably not the proper term. But you can maximise it, you can synergise it the way it's shown here, and this is the key mission of the commander: Taking the means available to him and make the maximum use out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I refer you to the second document, which is a document called, "Integration of Combat Functions," paragraph 66 of this document refers exactly to what you have just mentioned, which is: "The multiple combinations of the combat functions are designed by the commander to produce maximum combat power." Could you refer to paragraph 67 and see whether "Main effort," without -- whether this name can be employed or not, whether the first paragraph determines a very important part of maximising combat power.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fast-reading class I'm undergoing right now. It really stresses very much on my mental flexibility. But I'll try to do it. I think the key thing which is said here is that you have to -- to concentrate the forces available to you on one main objective; i.e., to -- to channelise everything you have and not to disperse your forces. The more you have a main effort, the more successful you might be. And therefore, we always go for a main effort, and to find the main effort is one of the key missions or -- or to define the main effort is one of the key missions of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we refer to page 2 of this document, which paragraph 71 on the top, about synchronisation. Could you elaborate on paragraph 71 and what is meant by the "synchronisation."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think "synchronisation" sounds very easy, but it's probably the most difficult part in the execution of the operation because you have different -- a different kind of forces to do the job, and you have air forces, you have far-reaching artillery, you have helicopters, what have you, and all these have to be synchronised in time on your main emphasis. And to do this time-wise and also organisation-wise is a very heavy burden and really makes the guts out of the capability of a commander, whether he's capable of doing that, and not piecemealing his forces into business.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you relate, General, to the line 3 of the paragraph 71, where it is mentioned: "He is attacked or threatened from so many angles at once that he is denied the ability to concentrate on one problem at a time or to establish priorities and facing menacing dilemmas about how and where to react, he is torn in different directions. Even if not totally paralysed, he finds it hard to respond to coherently and in a timely manner." Can you relate this description.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you're not torn to pieces. I'm still here in my entity; and General Hadzihasanovic as well. So, sure, this is right. In [indiscernible] operations, this is very difficult. But let's stress again that you're not constantly day and night, over days and weeks and months in operations. There are operational pauses, and then it might be necessary to take over some of the things which you had to delay during the operations and catch up and try to solve the problems then. So this is absolutely true in the peak of operations, that you basically concentrate and leave everything aside, but this doesn't preclude you from doing things which you are entitled to do or which you think are necessary to do afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the last part on paragraph 74, with respect to tempo, it says exactly what you've mentioned, that: "The tempo will also be a determinate -- a determining factor."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the last page of this document, where we have an illustration again of the same three principles or combat functions into a drawing, would you agree that this is -- when you compare the desired end state that you will exercise main effort, synchronisation, and tempo in order to apply maximum combat power?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this picture here is a good explanation of what you actually have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender the first page of the document with the diagram, just the first page, because the rest does not matter, so only the first page with the document, with three pages, "Integration of combat forces." I would like to have a number, one number for the two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on, General Reinhardt, in terms of the responsibilities of a commander. Would you agree with me that if I tried to take all responsibilities of a commanding general and to divide them into three categories: Responsibilities towards the chain of command and the state; responsibilities towards the troops and the subordinates; and legal responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at the first type of responsibility, which is responsibility towards the chain of command and the state, would I be right in talking about -- in this respect, the supremacy of the mission as being the focus of the commanding general?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it, General, that you are familiar with the principles of war?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're read my Clausewitz. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like -- I would like to show you a document, General, which basically is a comparison between the principles of war as applied in a number of different armies in order to compare. Looking at this diagram, first could you explain to the Trial Chamber what is meant by the "principles of war"?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I really I have to look through this diagram first. I see it for the first time. It's a rather complicated thing. I'm an old general; I'm a retired general; it takes me a little bit more time. But I think the principles of war, if I'd like to elaborate on that, are principles which are applicable, notwithstanding which army it is, notwithstanding which kind of operations it is, which apply historically throughout our -- our perception of war, and this is that you normally have to be effective, that you have to have a main emphasis, that you have to use maximum surprise on the enemy on securing your own forces, that you have to be very flexible, and that the -- that the war is normally a part of the overall strategy of a country, of a state. So surprise, security, concentration of forces is a key thing on the battleground, but it -- it's based on the morale of the soldiers. If you don't have the morale, if you don't have the discipline, if the soldiers don't want to obey your orders because they are disillusioned or so, all the other principles don't fit into the business. They don't materialise, I would rather say. So I think one of the key problems in all wars, notwithstanding whether it is Alexander the Great or a war of today is how to maintain the moral on the highest level, because this is your biggest asset.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if I can refer you to -- in terms of line 1 of this page, it talks about under "Canadian Forces," the number one principle of war as being "selection and maintenance of the aim." That appears to be the same for the British Army. That objective would be that for the United States Army, "advance and consolidation" for the USSR Army - now, you can see that this is an old document - and the People's Republic of China as being the aim of war is "singleness of direction." Would you agree with me, General, that this is -- for all these five different countries, that this means the same?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you relate to this principle?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain what would be meant by "selection and maintenance of the aim."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is that you decide your main emphasis and you concentrate everything on that main emphasis, which is the objective always is the maintenance of the aim or the singleness of the direction; that is, you have one key objective on which you coordinate all your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I refer you to the second page of this document, at the bottom, where we talk about the ten principles of war and we talk about paragraph 5(a), "Selection and maintenance of the aim," where it says that: "In the conduct of war, as a whole and in every operation of war it is essential to select and define the aim clearly. The ultimate aim is to break the enemy's will to fight." But my -- the issue I'd like to raise with you is five lines from the bottom, where it says that: "The selection and maintenance of the aim must be regarded as the master principle and has therefore been placed first. The remaining principles are not given any particular order since their relative importance will vary according to the nature of the operation in question." Would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is very academic, but the reality shows that this normally, under normal principles, you go for the enemy's will to fight, but it can be -- very well be just that you have the second principle, making it the first principle. Henry V, when he fought the French in Agincourt, he basically had a much larger army in front of him, he was totally outnumbered, but based on the maintenance of his morale he defeated a much higher and much, much more efficient army just on the principle of morale. So it -- it really can be a different way where you just wage the principles of war differently; therefore, that this is the master principle, this is one key principle, but you really have to play with the elements which you have depending on the situation, depending on the enemy on -- on the opposite number -- on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if I can put my question another way as being the master principle, what I'm referring to is the ultimate importance of the mission, which would be determined by the application of all the other principles.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, the mission is your key direction under which you basically concentrate everything you're doing. You always have the mission which is given from higher headquarters as your basic azimuth of what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
