utterances.text: Now, if I may allow, General, from -- one question related to the facts. Like I said, tomorrow will be more a factual day. But from the documents that you have read, have you identified what would have been General Hadzihasanovic's mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his key mission was to defend against the HVO and Bosnian Serb forces, his own country, and to make sure that as few as possible of his Muslim brothers and citizens in the area are -- have been molested. So his main emphasis was to liberate -- to liberate those forces and those people in the area of which he had responsibility from attack from two sources attacking him at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender this document into evidence. I would like to have a number for it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, the Prosecution has no objection to this document being admitted into evidence. We would, again, ask for the source of this document to be provided to us in due course. I'm also not sure if perhaps my learned colleague can comment on the fact that the document on the bottom of page 2, at least, seems to indicate that it's restricted. I don't know if this document is otherwise in the public domain. Perhaps that's linked to the source of the document, but I simply draw that to the Trial Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does say "restricted" on page 2. What is the provenance of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is from the Canadian Forces, and the security code of the document is restricted. I don't know exactly, but there are different codes. There are documents which do not have any classification. The first level is the restricted diffusion. It can be secret and very secret. The documents which are restricted are limited, there is limited diffusion of the documents. However, there's no problem for us using it. But my learned friend does have a point here. He is not aware of the source, but we will inform them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit DH150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General Reinhardt, I'm moving on. Of course, that was the upward responsibility, but there's also a downward responsibility. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the downward responsibility, I'm not sure about the German Army, but at least in the Canadian Army it is an ongoing dilemma as to is there such a thing as loyalty from the commander to the troops. What would your reading of this -- what would you answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wonder about the question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if there was a situation in which a commander was placed between what you say is the loyalty to the troops and loyalty to the chain of command, which one would come first?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he has to go for the loyalty of the chain of command because this is his basic mission, but I think this is very academic, the way you try to split it up. Because you can accomplish your mission only with the troops on your hands. And if they're not loyal to you, your loyalty towards the mission of the state cannot be executed. So this is mutually supporting. And that applies to General Hadzihasanovic, like to any other general. You know, you really have to have the loyalty of your troops, because they have to sacrifice their life, they have to go into combat, into fire. And normally they don't go into combat for any big terms, like liberty and things like this; they go most of the time into combat on loyalty for their brothers-in-arms and for their commander. If they don't believe in their commander, they will not follow you. So this is a thing which I'm very, very hesitant to say, this is priority number 1, this is priority number 2. I think it's mutually supporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this sense, General, would you agree with me that in this mutual supporting or supportive role that the commander as a minimum has a duty to his troops to optimise their chances of survival and to maximise the security of his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in doing so the commander will enhance cohesion, confidence, and morale of his troops?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But in the same respect, when and should there be a conflict, he will have to have the chain of command come first.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, that was the downward responsibilities. Now, of course, we come to the legal responsibilities. And from reading your report, I guess you will agree with me that the legal responsibilities of a commander is first and foremost to respect the law.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that includes the national laws, including degrees -- decrees, sorry, regulations, as well as binding army regulations.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the commander must also respect international law.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If it applies, of course.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he has to respect it, and most of the time the national law forces him to respect the international law, and it's amazing how much stress the new Bosnian government has put on this question of international law and the humanitarian law and made their soldiers aware of how important it is for the new country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you referring in this comment to 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. For me it was amazing seeing all those documents that in such a difficult situation Bosnia was at that time how much stress was put on making sure that the soldiers fighting the battles are obliged to adhere to the rules of international law. I think this was a very important thing, and it really struck me how much -- how much importance has been given by that -- to that by the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that it is also the commander's obligation to ensure that his subordinates of course respect and apply the law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So not only the state has to do it but the commander also -- also needs to do it.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will also agree with me that it is the commander's obligation or duty when there are breaches to the law to see that these -- that he suppress and repress, if necessary, these breaches.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he has to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is his duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's his duty to suppress them and to prevent repetitions of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And because we mentioned earlier that the focus of the commander was on his mission, would I be right in saying that all the good things we have said about mission, about focus, about the difficulties of the commander, that this must always be done within the confines of the law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in this respect, the law is the left and right boundaries of military action.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: However, that they will not be the focus of the commander as long as -- as he is within those boundaries.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to a section that also deals with the responsibilities of the commander, and that basically deals with accountability versus criminal liability. You have said in your report that a commander -- the commanding general is responsible for everything. Do you see a difference in this respect between accountability of a commander and the criminal responsibility of a commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I say he is responsible for everything in his area of responsibility, I think that covers criminal aspects as well as disciplinary and operational aspects. So everything, it's everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But do you figure that accountability is the same as criminal liability?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you, I think I'm not -- I'm not good enough to really differentiate between those two terms. I don't -- I'm not firm enough in your language to see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document, General Reinhardt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to bring this document. The reference of this document is -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I thought you had the document. Sorry, I will wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that there's not enough copies for everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This document, General Reinhardt, is -- the reference is from the Canadian National Defence, and this is from the chief of the defence staff, and this is guidance to commanding officers taken out of 1999 and 2000, Book 1, and this is an executive summary. And what we see in this document, the first part, which I put in bold: "The responsibilities of an officer may involve the most hazardous and demanding circumstances and of course carries with it the responsibility for the lives of their people and the understanding of their risk, which are at the core of every officer's responsibilities and competency." Would you agree with such a statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At paragraph 105.2, direction of guidance given is: "You must abide by all prevailing laws, regulations, rules, and policies." And I leave you to read the rest of this quote. But would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that, talking about the responsibilities at paragraph 203.1, the part in bold, it is mentioned that: "You have responsibilities to your service, to the Canadian Forces, the nation, and humanity in general, and that whether in peacetime or on operations, a commander, by force of his personality, leadership, command style, and general behaviour has considerable influence on the morale, sense of direction, and performance of his staff and subordinate commanders." Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's almost identical what I said before on the high importance of the morale of the soldiers and your staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the second page of this document, which basically talks about authority, responsibility, and accountability. And in the first paragraph, we talk about: "As a commanding officer you are accountable for achieving results and for doing so within prevailing laws." And then we go on to explain what is meant by "accountability." Meaning that accountability is you are responsible for what happens and everything that takes place within your unit. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that criminal liability is different in terms of if a commander commits a crime, this will entail his criminal liability?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we have mentioned -- or in your report you have mentioned that there was such a thing as a vertical chain of command in that each commander up the chain of command in the same chain were responsible for one another.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to mention one example to you. And again, it comes from Canada, whereas in Somalia Canadian soldiers committed some violations, whereas a Somali was tortured to death by two soldiers. Going up the chain of command, the soldiers who committed the torture were charged and court-martialled. The sergeant who was on duty that night was charged and court-martialled. The duty officer, a captain, was also charged, even though he had nothing to do with the act, on the basis because he was the duty officer. And the commanding officer of the commando or the company at that time was also charged in relation to the torturing of a Somali. However, the commander of the unit was not charged. Based on your experience, could you see a reason why the commander of the unit was not charged?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reason I would see is that the commander of the unit by the time this happened did not know about the incident and that once he has known about the incident has taken all the means necessary to investigate and to prevent further happening. So I would say that this commander has taken the appropriate steps once he was informed what happened, while the ones who were charged were the ones who knew what happened and did -- were involved in these happenings. This is my explanation. I don't know whether the explanation is right, but this will be my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in this respect, I would like to provide you with two further examples: The first one where yourself in your capacity as German national commander for a number of deployments. Would you agree with me that during those deployments, breaches of the law did take place by German soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you were not -- never in any way charged or had any judicial procedures taken against you for such breaches.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you were nevertheless responsible for those breaches.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But whenever I heard about something like this, I started investigation right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that in a sense that at some point in the chain of command when it can be determined that a commanding general acted reasonably, took the necessary and reasonable measures in the circumstances, that in such a case he is no longer criminally responsible?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I relate to your own example in Kosovo, where you were a commander of KFOR, I relate to one incident of a -- if I take it -- I believe it was a murder that was committed by a United States member -- a member of the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And measures were taken.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not by yourself but by the United States military, because they were responsible for the disciplinary aspect.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But also by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were not in any way involved in any judicial proceedings about this event.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in the judicial --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Involved yourself, I mean.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- proceeding. But I tell you this was a big thing for the KFOR forces, and I really dug very much into that business and spent a lot of time to make sure that things like this would not happen and that the perpetrator was -- was pursued by his country accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you took the necessary and reasonable measures in the circumstances to ensure that the matter would be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in that respect, there was -- there was never an issue that your personal liability --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- would be involved.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to refer to you [sic] to some of -- some quotes that I found in some war crimes trial simply to know whether you would agree with these quotes as applying or being an application of what I've just mentioned. And the first one would be -- it comes from the Yamashita judgement again. And I refer here to this -- to the test as being the commander -- sorry, where the commander -- and I quote from page 169. No, this is 169 of an article, I'm sorry. I would have to quote from -- this is footnote 53, and that would be -- I will provide the reference later, but it comes from the Yamashita judgement, and it says: "Where the commander deviates significantly from customary command practices and war crimes are committed by subordinates as a direct result, the commander may be guilty of underlying offences just as if he had committed them himself." Can you comment on this quote, not again -- not from a legal perspective, from a command perspective.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the case being as you just described it, the commander knew about criminal offences. He did not intervene. He let them go, so in this case I think, yes, he is reliable and accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to refer you to a different quote, this time in the High Command case, and in this case we find the following rationale: "Military subordination is a comprehensive but not conclusive factor in fixing criminal responsibility. A high commander cannot keep completely informed of the details of military operations of subordinates. He has the right to assume that details entrusted to responsible subordinates will be legally executed." Would you agree with this quote from a command perspective?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it goes on to say: "There must be a personal dereliction that can only occur where the act is directly traceable to him or where his failure to properly supervise his subordinates constitute criminal negligence on his part." From a command perspective, would you agree with this quote?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the negligence part is the key question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it goes on to say- and this is my last - "In the latter case, it must be a personal neglect amounting to a wanton immoral disregard for the action of his subordinates, amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of international law would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law as known to civilised nations." From a command perspective, would you agree with this quote?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- could you repeat the quote. I think -- I think I just didn't -- I just didn't get it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I see time running by. It's my mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... quote again, and it goes: "In the latter case, it must be a personal neglect amounting to a wanton immoral disregard of the action of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of international law would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law as known to civilised nations."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is on a very high level and very abstract, I must say, but basically yes, I think I would go with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, in your written report - and I refer you to a specific paragraph in your report - where you deal with the actions that must be taken by a commander. And I take it that -- I think this is an issue that comes, again, into one more place in your report. Paragraph 2.14.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is at the top of page 5. So I'll start with -- sorry, with the bottom of page 4, so we have the full paragraph, so we don't -- "A commander has to investigate and to initiate appropriate actions as soon as he becomes aware of alleged or de facto criminal activities or acts violating international law committed by individuals or units in his area of responsibility." Now, your reference in this case is the German Military Disciplinary Code. I can refer you to the exact section of the Penal Code, but may I suggest to you that the words "as soon as he becomes aware" are not found in the German Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I didn't quote verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you go on in this respect by saying that: "By individuals or units in his area of responsibility." Now, you recall that yesterday we discussed that the only legal provision that you could find concerning area of responsibility was of no application and that there were no other that you could find which talked about area of responsibility. Should that be so -- because, of course, it is for the Trial Chamber to determine whether that is the situation or not. But should that be the situation, in the sense that the area of responsibility is not to be found in a legal text, would you agree with me that what is the test is the applicable international law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no question about the applicable of the international law [sic]. But I think the way you interpret what I said yesterday is too exclusive. What I talked about yesterday in this law which you said is not applicable, the JNA law on the rules of the application of international law, it says that the commander is responsible also for the things done by units under his command and even individuals not under his command, in his area of responsibility. So for me it's not the question of the area of responsibility which I was quoting yesterday in -- I think it's Article 21 of this regulation, but it's -- it's the question of responsibility for things done by subordinates and even non-subordinates but somehow operating in his area of responsibility. I think area of responsibility is found more often in the different legal papers I have -- I went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, if I suggest to you that -- that "area of responsibility" and "acts committed by others" is not the applicable standard, neither in national law or international law - I just suggest to you - are you telling me that on your -- on the basis of your professional experience you are talking about area of responsibility or are you talking area of responsibility and others as a matter of law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is not exclusive. I think you are given an area of responsibility as a commander with troops, with a geographical limit for which you are responsible, and everything which happens in that area has a legal aspect to the things you are responsible for. So I don't see this exclusively as you see that. I think -- well, I don't want to repeat it. I just -- I just tried to explain myself. This is the way I interpret this, the way I was trained and educated to -- to see the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question, just to finalise on this issue: Do you see a difference between a commander who is in occupation, occupying a territory as being responsible for what happened in his area and a commander who is not into an occupying mode?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he must have the means to effect -- to have effective control over the forces in the area and over the area he is responsible for; otherwise, if he's just been given an area without the means to control it, he can't execute what he's supposed to do. So again, this both is somewhere very closely supplementary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what if the -- in the area of responsibility a civilian authority, as we discussed earlier today, was still -- the civil authorities were still operating --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- and that they are responsible for what he is not responsible for as a commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as criminal activities are being committed by civil -- by civilians, they are being dealt with by the still-existing civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I leave it at that, General. I just now go on to, again, the top of this paragraph, where you go on to say: "In this case, he must immediately initiate an investigation." And you quote paragraph 18 -- footnote 18 in Section 46 of the German Penal Code. May I suggest to you that Section 46 of the German Penal Code does not refer to "immediately initiate." Would I be correct? I could refer you to the German Penal Code, but would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The things which are in 56 are the bullets which I -- which follow here. This is the way I'm -- I've been trained, based on the German law, that if something happens like this, I as a commander have to react as soon as possible as I know that, and maybe immediately might be too harsh on that, but this is at least my understanding, that you have to react as soon as something is in your knowledge in this regard. You cannot defer it, because it's too important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this respect - because you say that this is the way that you were trained - so you're not saying that this is what the law requires.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know right now whether the law says "immediately," but the law says all these bullets which follow afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that would be in footnote 18.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Section 46.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because I have Section 46 here, and I think it is important that we take --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel come to the microphone, please. Could counsel come to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only five more minutes, Mr. President. I believe that it is very important for me to pursue in order to clarify this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... German Penal Code just so we can clarify this matter. Can you take it from the material that is with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, we don't have the text. Perhaps you would be kind enough to read to us Article 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I shall read Article 46. It is a text drafted in English, and it reads as follows: [In English] Supervision, senior -- [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the best idea would be to put the text on the ELMO so that everyone can see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... if you could put it on the device immediately to your right, the ELMO, so that everyone can see Section 46. And, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the Article 46 of the German Penal Code, disciplinary code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's not the Penal Code. It's the disciplinary code. I see, the disciplinary code of the German Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is the reference given by the witness in his report at footnote 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] If I read this text, you have the German in front of you, would I be right in saying that what this section refers to is what a senior disciplinary superior can do with respect to measures that were taken by a first-level disciplinary superior?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or not taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Or not taken.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, or not taken -- I'd like you to refer to me as to where it says "not taken," because I don't see that in Section 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the ELMO, we have the German text. Could we have the English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the text in French. Only I've marked it in colour. If my colleagues accept, I can have that one placed onto the overhead projector. Mr. President, this is the text, headed "Supervision." And I'm reading it: "The definition of the senior disciplinary superior is given earlier on." [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "in the exercise of their disciplinary authority." [Interpretation] And the Article continues regarding disciplinary superiors who issue disciplinary measures and what can be done to cancel them. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... so that we have the full -- and even if we go up -- [Interpretation] If we move it further up, we will see that nothing is stated in this section that refers to measures that need to be taken if the first disciplinary level has not taken any measures. [In English] Could you switch to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, my point is not whether -- I mean, this is -- this is the law. The Chamber is there to interpret the law. And in addition, this is German law. My point is not this. My point was simply that in this code of discipline, which is your national German provision, the idea of these measures that you're talking about in paragraph 2.14 are not there, but I take it that this is the way you were trained.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I think I have to say again. This is not a verbatim quotation from that as you see this in the bullets. And if you look into 17, footnote 17, I say, "This is between section 28 and 41." These are the measures which I basically deduct from the contents of my law. The way I've interpreted it, the way I had done this, and as I say, you have to make an immediate investigation based on Article 46 to do that. I did not -- I did not want to say that this is the -- some kind of verbatim of 48. This is the condensed or condensation of the measures I as a German commander would be responsible to take based on 21 to 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. But the only issue I was trying to bring about is that in neither of these sections, from 28 to 41, including 46, the issue of area of responsibility and the issue of immediately are, in my view, not there.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- issue of debate. I just wanted to bring that up.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediately" is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the issue of "immediately," I'd like to read you a quote, which I took from a -- an article written by a former United States marine who has become a very well-known writer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, we should finish soon. It's five to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Mr. President. I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please finish off, because we can't stay over 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of this law article, the author is Mr. Hays Parks, and he basically reviews the theory of prompt investigation. And he says that: "To the commander whose forces are heavily engaged in an intense operation or pitch battle, no reasonable means may exist to secure prompt punishment of an offence prior to the conclusion of that engagement. The theory of prompt investigation, trial, and punishment will be more stringently applied to a commander in a static tactical situation than one in a very fluid fast-moving situation which requires complete devotion to the accomplishment of the mission at hand." Would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't contradict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you repeat? I'm sorry, I--

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not contradict it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my last question simply is: Can you confirm that when a commander, a commanding general, has been shown not to have himself committed a crime and he has not -- and he has acted reasonably and necessary in the circumstances, that this commanding general should not incur criminal liability?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You imply something right now and want an answer which is very difficult, because as I said before, you are not constantly in the situation as you quoted it before. There are pauses in the operations. You are not six months constantly under this kind of stress. So I -- I basically agreed to what you have said before under that particular stress of a battle. But the question is: Will this continue or will this discontinue? And then you have an operational pause or something like this, where you can catch up what you could not have done beforehand, and I think this is the important thing I want -- I want -- we will have to see that what you have just said is absolutely right but it's not constantly a way in which a commander is under this kind of battle stress and battle fatigue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And therefore, would it be fair to say that you have to look at all the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- everything that was done, all the situations in order to assess that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, there's a document whose fate we don't know. It's a document entitled, "Authority, Responsibility and Accountability." What are we going to do with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd rather not tender it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, today's hearing, which was longer by 15 minutes than planned, is closing. General Reinhardt, please come back tomorrow for the hearing, which will start at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, of course, as I told you yesterday, from now until then you shouldn't have any contact with any party. Thank you very much. We will meet again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
